Where it began

Allan Donald was born in Bloemfontein on 20 October 1966 and grew up playing cricket, football and rugby. As a schoolboy he once took 9 for 16, against Grey College in Bloemfontein, his uncle's school. His first-class debut, for Orange Free State in November 1985, came out of the blue: named twelfth man, he was told he was playing by his captain, Chris Broad, about ten minutes before the toss. He was 19.

Warwickshire signed him in 1987 and he stayed until 2000. In 1991 he took 83 Championship wickets at 19.68, and in 1995 he helped the county to the County Championship and the NatWest Trophy in the same summer.

The player

When South Africa came back to international cricket in November 1991, at Eden Gardens, Donald took five Indian wickets in his first one-day international. His Test debut followed in Barbados in April 1992. On Boxing Day that year he took 12 wickets against India and South Africa won by nine wickets. In 1994 he put his name on the honours board at Lord's.

He was relentless. In 1998 he took 80 Test wickets in the calendar year, the most by anyone that year, and that summer at Trent Bridge he bowled a spell at Michael Atherton that both men later wrote about as among the most intense they ever played in. In November 2000 he reached 300 Test wickets, a first for a South African. He finished with 330 in 72 Tests, at 22.25 each, with 20 five-wicket innings and a best of 8 for 71.

What made him special

Pure pace and plenty of fire, which is how he earned the name White Lightning. Atherton fell to him 11 times in 17 Tests against each other. From the 1996–97 tour of India Donald shared the new ball with Shaun Pollock, and the two became firm friends; Donald once described Pollock as South Africa's Glenn McGrath, which from a fast bowler is high praise.

Batting was another matter. He began his Test career with a pair in Barbados, and his best score in 72 Tests was 37. Bowlers were never too worried to see him walk out.

Away from the middle

He became one of the game's most sought-after coaches. He was a bowling consultant to England in 2007, worked with Warwickshire, New Zealand and Kent, and was South Africa's bowling coach from 2011 to the 2015 World Cup, later taking on the same job for Bangladesh. He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, and in 2019 he entered the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame.

And finally

Fans remember the face as well as the bowling: he played with bright zinc cream smeared across his cheeks and nose to keep off the sun. It made him easy to spot from the far end of any ground, which, for a batsman, was not always good news.
